messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir was seven the first time his father’s open hand caught him across the face hard enough to knock him to the kitchen floor. There was no warning—just a flash of heat and a ringing in his ear that lasted through dinner. The beatings continued for years, always unannounced, always over something Amir could not predict: a dish left unwashed, a word spoken too softly, a silence his father read as defiance. By the time he left home at eighteen, Amir had learned that safety meant never relaxing, never turning his back, never assuming that a quiet room would stay quiet.

Now, at nineteen and newly married, Amir works as an environmental scientist for a small consulting firm. His job requires him to spend hours in a shared office or out in the field with colleagues, and every setting feels layered with unseen threat. When voices rise in a meeting—even a friendly debate over sampling methods—Amir’s stomach knots and his hands go cold. The sound of a coworker crying in the breakroom after a personal call sends a spike of adrenaline through him, and he will leave the floor rather than pass near the door. Most intrusively, being touched unexpectedly, even a tap on the shoulder from a teammate asking for a file, makes him flinch and step back, heart pounding as if the touch were a blow.

Amir has come to believe that the world is filled with hidden danger, and that only constant vigilance can keep him safe. He studies every face that enters a room, scanning for the narrowing of eyes or the tightening of a jaw that might signal anger or rejection. In meetings he chooses a seat with his back to the wall, and at lunch he positions himself so he can see the door and everyone around him. This hypervigilance narrows his attention: he is so focused on detecting threat that he often misreads neutral expressions as hostile, and the very act of scanning makes him notice potential triggers—a colleague’s raised eyebrow, a sudden silence—that others would ignore.

To manage the constant sense of danger, Amir has developed a tight set of rules. He avoids any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, so he never speaks up in meetings even when his data is questioned, and he defers to whoever seems most assertive. He avoids being alone in a room or building, because when he is by himself there is no one to watch for him, and the silence feels like waiting. Most of all, he avoids people: he eats lunch at his desk with his back to the wall, he takes the stairs instead of the elevator to minimize chance encounters, and he has stopped accepting invitations to colleague gatherings. But these strategies backfire. His silence frustrates coworkers, who interpret it as disinterest or incompetence, and their irritation leads to sharper words that Amir reads as signs of imminent attack—which only deepens his avoidance. When he comes home to his wife, he is so wound up that a simple question about his day feels like an interrogation, and he lashes out or withdraws, sparking arguments that he then must escape from by leaving the room. His wife’s tears, once a source of comfort, now feel like a trigger, and he cannot bear to see her cry without his pulse racing.

Amir has not slept through a night in months. He has started asking for solo field assignments to avoid people, but the isolation makes him jump at every rustle of wind. He sought help only after his supervisor pulled him aside and said his evasiveness was affecting team morale and his performance review was at risk. What Amir does not say is that he is terrified of losing his job, which would mean returning home to his wife full-time, where her presence would be constant and he would have no escape from the vigilance that exhausts him. He hopes, vaguely, that therapy can give him a few hours of peace—a room where his back is not to the wall, and where no one will cry or touch him without warning.
